title: Lost Procedures, GPS Navigation, and Diversion Decision-Making

questions.text: A pilot experiences complete two-way radio failure while operating VFR in Class D airspace and planning to land at the Class D airport. What transponder code should be set, and what arrival procedure applies?

options.label: A
options.text: Set 7700 (emergency) — two-way radio failure in Class D airspace constitutes an in-flight emergency under 14 CFR 91.3; squawk emergency first, then follow 14 CFR 91.185 NORDO arrival procedures to land as quickly as possible

options.label: B
options.text: Set 7600 (radio failure) — two-way radio failure alone is not an emergency; 14 CFR 91.185 provides a specific NORDO procedure: remain VFR, observe the traffic pattern, watch for light gun signals from the tower, and land if cleared by a green light signal

options.label: C
options.text: Set 1200 (standard VFR) — two-way radio failure does not require a special transponder code; the pilot should enter the traffic pattern normally and land without tower clearance, as radio communication is advisory-only at Class D airports under FAR 91.126

options.label: D
options.text: Set 7500 (hijack) — radio loss during an airport approach is classified as an unlawful interference event by the FAA because it may indicate an electronic warfare threat; the hijack code alerts military resources to escort the aircraft to the ground safely

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.185 provides the specific procedure for two-way radio communication failure during VFR conditions: the pilot should continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable, squawking 7600 to signal the radio failure. Light gun signals are the primary communication medium: a steady green light while in the pattern means 'cleared to land.' VFR radio failure is not automatically an emergency — it is a communication anomaly with a defined procedure. Squawking 7700 (Option A) would declare an emergency unnecessarily and potentially compromise separation services for other aircraft. Option C incorrectly dismisses the need for the 7600 code and misapplies 91.126 (uncontrolled airport rules) to Class D — Class D requires radio communication by 91.129, and NORDO procedures must be followed. Option D is extremely wrong — radio failure is never classified as a hijack event.

questions.text: Under 14 CFR 91.225, in which of the following airspace situations is ADS-B Out equipment NOT required?

options.label: A
options.text: Operating in Class E airspace at 8,000 feet MSL over the continental United States

options.label: B
options.text: Operating in Class B airspace, regardless of altitude

options.label: C
options.text: Operating within 30 nautical miles of a Class B primary airport from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL

options.label: D
options.text: Operating in Class E airspace at 3,000 feet MSL over the Gulf of Mexico within 12 nm of the coastline

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.225 requires ADS-B Out in: Class A airspace (all altitudes), Class B airspace (all altitudes), Class C airspace (all altitudes), Class E airspace at and above 10,000 feet MSL (excluding operations below 2,500 feet AGL), the Mode C veil (within 30 nm of Class B primary airports, surface to 10,000 feet MSL), Class E airspace over the Gulf of Mexico at and above 3,000 feet MSL within 12 nm of the U.S. coastline. Critically NOT required: Class E airspace BELOW 10,000 feet MSL (except the Gulf provision and the Mode C veil). A pilot operating in Class E at 8,000 feet MSL over the continental United States (but not in the Mode C veil of a Class B airport) is in airspace where ADS-B Out is NOT required. This is a common exam trap — many pilots assume ADS-B Out is required in all Class E airspace.

questions.text: A VFR pilot becomes uncertain of position 25 minutes into a cross-country flight. The last confirmed landmark was a large lake 10 minutes ago. The pilot's current altitude is 3,500 feet MSL, approximately 1,500 feet AGL. Which action BEST demonstrates the 3C lost procedure?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue on the planned heading at 3,500 feet MSL while attempting to identify landmarks below — maintaining the flight plan heading gives the best probability of reaching the next planned waypoint and regaining positional awareness within the next 5 to 10 minutes

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately squawk 7700 and declare an emergency on 121.5 MHz — positional uncertainty in VFR flight constitutes an emergency under 14 CFR 91.3, and ATC radar vectors are the fastest way to re-establish position through official channels

options.label: C
options.text: Climb to at least 4,500 feet AGL, circle over the most recently identified geographic feature visible, attempt to identify current position using pilotage, and if position cannot be confirmed, contact ATC or FSS on 121.5 for assistance while managing fuel conservation

options.label: D
options.text: Descend to 1,000 feet AGL to achieve better landmark visibility and identify roads and towns more precisely — low-altitude flight provides better visual resolution of ground features and restores navigational confidence faster than climbing

questions.explanation: Option C correctly applies the 3C lost procedure in sequence: (1) CLIMB to improve horizon visibility for landmark identification and extend VHF radio range — 4,500 feet AGL recommended, observing 91.119 terrain clearance. (2) CIRCLE over the last visible geographic feature to halt positional error growth. (3) COMMUNICATE if position cannot be confirmed from the climb and circle — contact ATC or FSS on 121.5 MHz for radar identification. Also CONSERVE fuel by avoiding large course deviations. Option A continues the positional error — pressing forward when lost may take the aircraft further from known terrain and into hazardous airspace. Option B over-escalates — positional uncertainty alone is not an emergency; ATC services are appropriate but 7700 is premature. Option D descending is operationally dangerous: reduces terrain clearance, reduces radio range, and in hilly terrain significantly increases CFIT risk.

questions.text: A VFR pilot's EFB displays a RAIM alert during cruise. The GPS is flagging insufficient satellite geometry for navigation integrity. What is the correct response?

options.label: A
options.text: Ignore the alert for VFR navigation — RAIM alerts are technically relevant only for IFR approaches in Class B and C airspace; VFR GPS accuracy degradation of even 500 feet is operationally acceptable for enroute position awareness

options.label: B
options.text: Continue navigating but note the alert in the flight log and report it to the FBO upon landing — RAIM alerts are informational warnings that require documentation but do not require in-flight navigation changes for Part 91 VFR operations

options.label: C
options.text: Revert to pilotage and dead reckoning immediately to maintain independent position awareness — a RAIM alert means the GPS receiver cannot verify its own accuracy; trusting a RAIM-alerting GPS for position could produce position errors of miles without any further indication

options.label: D
options.text: Switch to an alternate GPS frequency — RAIM alerts indicate the GPS is operating on a degraded frequency band; switching between GPS satellite constellations via the EFB settings menu will restore signal integrity and resolve the alert within 30 to 60 seconds of frequency selection

questions.explanation: A RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) alert indicates the GPS receiver has detected insufficient satellite geometry to guarantee navigation accuracy. When RAIM alerts, the GPS position display may be significantly off — by hundreds of feet to miles — with no reliable way for the pilot to know the magnitude of the error. The correct response is to immediately revert to independent navigation (pilotage from landmarks, dead reckoning using last known position + heading + time) and treat the GPS position as unreliable until the alert clears. Option A falsely restricts RAIM applicability to IFR phases — RAIM is relevant anytime GPS is the primary navigation tool. Option B treats a navigation integrity failure as documentation-only rather than an immediate operational response. Option D invents a 'frequency switching' capability that does not exist in aviation GPS receivers — RAIM is managed by satellite geometry, not frequency selection.

questions.text: A pilot is 45 minutes into a 2-hour cross-country. The AWOS at the destination airport is now reporting OVC009 and 3/4SM in fog — below the VFR minimums the pilot had planned for. The pilot has 3.5 hours of fuel. What is the CORRECT application of the three-step diversion model?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue to the destination — the AWOS is reporting current conditions; by the time the 75-minute remaining ETE elapses, the morning fog will likely have burned off, and VFR conditions will be available; 3.5 hours of fuel provides ample time to hold if needed

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately declare fuel minimum and enter a hold over the nearest VOR — with fog at the destination, the pilot should enter a holding pattern at the nearest VOR for up to 2 hours waiting for VFR conditions, using the 3.5-hour fuel reserve for the extended hold

options.label: C
options.text: Apply the pre-set personal decision trigger (destination VFR below 2,000 AGL / 3 SM), identify the nearest suitable VFR airport within current fuel state, verify its conditions via radio weather, and divert while fuel state and weather options are still favorable

options.label: D
options.text: Contact Approach Control and request a Special VFR clearance to operate to the destination below VFR minimums — Special VFR is available to Part 91 pilots in Class D airspace and allows completion of the planned flight even when weather conditions fall below standard VFR minimums

questions.explanation: Option C is the correct application of the three-step diversion model applied in favorable conditions: (1) TRIGGER has been reached — destination is below the pilot's pre-set personal minimum (OVC009 is 900 AGL, below the 2,000 AGL trigger). (2) SELECT ALTERNATE — with 3.5 hours of fuel and conditions that are clearly below VFR at destination, the pilot has ample fuel to identify and reach a suitable VFR alternate. (3) NAVIGATE — divert now, while fuel and weather options are good. Waiting 75 more minutes narrows both fuel margin and alternate options. Option A is classic Get-There-Itis — rationalizing continuation based on a weather guess rather than a data trigger. Option B is dangerous — 2 hours of holding burns most of the 3.5 hours of fuel and commits the pilot to eventually landing at an IMC airport or declaring an emergency. Option D is technically possible (Special VFR in Class D requires ATC clearance and 1 SM visibility/clear of clouds), but SVFR in 3/4 SM fog at night is high risk and is not the preferred decision model — diversion to VFR conditions is always preferable to SVFR operations near minimums. Part 91 pilots may request SVFR, but this scenario's trigger has already been reached.

questions.text: A student pilot mistakenly sets transponder code 7500 instead of 7600 during a simulated radio failure exercise with a CFI. The CFI realizes the error and tells the student to reset to 7600. What is the likely immediate consequence?

options.label: A
options.text: No immediate consequence — ATC transponder codes are advisory only; a brief 7500 squawk lasting under 30 seconds does not trigger any automated alert and will be dismissed as a transponder testing event once corrected

options.label: B
options.text: ATC will issue an immediate call on 121.5 MHz and may coordinate military intercept resources — a 7500 squawk triggers automated hijack response protocols; once set, the response cannot be canceled by a verbal radio call alone and typically requires the crew to squawk 7700 to confirm the error

options.label: C
options.text: ATC will call the aircraft on its assigned frequency to confirm the squawk — if the pilot verbally confirms radio capability and explains the error, ATC will log the event and no further action is taken; 7500 alerts have a mandatory 60-second delay before triggering military notification

options.label: D
options.text: The transponder will automatically reset to 1200 — modern transponders have a built-in safety check that prevents momentary 7500 squawk activation by student pilots; the avionics will revert to the previous code within 15 seconds if the 7500 code is not confirmed with a second button press

questions.explanation: Squawking 7500 (hijack) triggers an immediate, automatic response by ATC. The signal is treated as a hijack communication — ATC will attempt discrete radio contact first (to give the crew an opportunity to deny the squawk). However, the military coordination and notification procedures begin almost immediately. ATC cannot simply accept a radio transmission saying 'sorry, wrong code' as definitive proof the aircraft is not under threat — protocol requires continuing the response unless the crew demonstrates they have positive control of the aircraft by performing a specific squawk sequence. The standard procedure to confirm a 7500 squawk error is typically to squawk 7700, then the appropriate code — but this varies by facility. The core lesson: 7500 is never 'tested.' Option A falsely minimizes the impact. Option C invents a 60-second delay that does not exist. Option D invents a transponder safety interlock against 7500 that does not exist in any aircraft avionics system.

questions.text: A private pilot departed for a 150-nm cross-country under VFR. Forty miles from the destination, the pilot observes the horizon ahead becoming hazy and indistinct. The AWOS at the destination last reported (30 minutes ago) showed VFR conditions. The pilot's personal minimums card sets a diversion trigger at below 5 miles visibility at destination. The pilot thinks: 'It's probably just haze from a nearby city — I'll press on and check the next AWOS cycle in 10 minutes.' What ADM hazard is at work, and what is the safest action?

options.label: A
options.text: No hazard — extending evaluation time by 10 minutes is reasonable ADM; gathering additional data before making an irreversible decision to divert is consistent with risk management principles described in FAA-H-8083-2A

options.label: B
options.text: Get-There-Itis is at work — the pilot is rationalizing continuation through developing adverse weather by deferring the decision to the next data cycle rather than applying the pre-set trigger; the safest action is to immediately verify the destination conditions via radio PIREP or phone, simultaneously identify the best diversion alternate, and divert before the option window narrows further

options.label: C
options.text: Invulnerability is at work — the pilot is flying into a known deteriorating situation without a specific outcome in mind; the safest action is to climb to the cruise ceiling, activate the VFR flight plan, and continue at maximum altitude until destination conditions can be confirmed

options.label: D
options.text: Press-On-Itis is at work but is manageable — the 10-minute evaluation period is within FAA ADM acceptable variance; the pilot should simultaneously set the transponder to 7600 and contact ATC for a position and weather update before making any diversion decision at this stage

questions.explanation: This scenario demonstrates Get-There-Itis (also called Press-on Itis in the FAA's hazardous attitude taxonomy): the pilot has a pre-established trigger and the trigger conditions are developing, but is rationalizing a delay in applying it. The 10-minute wait is rational-sounding but its purpose is to avoid making the diversion decision — not to gather truly essential missing data. Useful weather data is already available: degrading visual horizon forward, a 30-minute-old AWOS that may not reflect current conditions. NTSB SS-15-01 identifies this exact rationalization pattern ('I'll wait one more cycle') as a predecessor event in over 40% of VFR-into-IMC fatal accident cases. The safest action: call Flight Service or an ASOS/AWOS in the area for updated PIREPs, confirm the nearest diversion airport conditions and fuel, and begin the diversion now — not in 10 minutes. The NTSB report (SS-15-01) identified that VFR-into-IMC accidents are 11.2x more likely to be fatal than other accident types.
questions.sjt_rationale: Get-There-Itis is the most lethal hazardous attitude in cross-country VFR flight. The rationalization 'one more data cycle' is the behavioral signature. Pre-set personal triggers exist specifically to remove this in-flight decision load — if the trigger is not honored, it is not a trigger. Reference: NTSB Safety Study SS-15-01.

questions.text: On a checkride cross-country, the DPE removes the sectional chart and EFB ('both are unavailable — you are lost'). The applicant says 'I'll look for a town and call ATC.' The DPE asks: 'What frequency? What will you say? What are you squawking?' The applicant is unable to answer specifically. What does this reveal, and what is the correct response to each question?

options.label: A
options.text: The applicant demonstrates appropriate uncertainty — verifying ATC frequencies live via EFB is the correct professional approach; the DPE's questions are designed to identify gaps in rote memory, which is not relevant to a pilot with working avionics in normal operations

options.label: B
options.text: The applicant reveals inadequate lost procedure knowledge — frequency: 121.5 MHz (emergency guard, monitored by ATC and FSS); call: '[All stations / ATC], [callsign], VFR aircraft uncertain of position, [type/altitude/last known position], request assistance'; squawk: 7700 if an emergency, continue 1200 if requesting assistance only; ATC will provide radar identification and vectors

options.label: C
options.text: The applicant reveals an EFB dependency — the correct answer is to squawk 7600 (radio failure) to inform ATC without declaring an emergency, contact ground FSS on 122.8 MHz for radar identity, and report position using GPS altitude and magnetic heading from the aircraft's internal navigation instruments

options.label: D
options.text: The applicant reveals complacency — the correct response is to first correct the DPE for creating a scenario without available materials, then explain the lost procedure from memory including using 122.2 MHz as the primary FSS frequency, squawking 7600, and orbiting the minimum IFR altitude shown on the low enroute chart

questions.explanation: The DPE's three questions test specific knowledge that must be available from memory — not from a device. The correct answers: (1) FREQUENCY: 121.5 MHz is the international aeronautical emergency frequency, monitored by all ATC facilities, FSS stations, and many commercial aircraft. It is the primary frequency for lost/distress communications in the United States. 122.1 MHz or 122.2 MHz are FSS communication frequencies (secondary option). (2) RADIO CALL: State who you are, what you are, where you are (last known position), what you need. Full call: '[Facility / All Stations], [Callsign], VFR [aircraft type], [altitude], uncertain of position, last known [landmark], request radar identification and assistance.' (3) SQUAWK: If a genuine emergency exists, 7700. If requesting assistance but not declaring an emergency, remain on 1200 and ATC will respond to the 121.5 call for radar identification. Option C incorrectly specifies 7600 (radio failure) — the radio is working in this scenario. Option D incorrectly specifies 7600 and references low IFR enroute procedures that are not applicable to a VFR lost situation.
questions.sjt_rationale: The failure to answer these questions from memory demonstrates that the applicant's 'lost procedure knowledge' was dependent on the EFB — precisely the training gap the DPE is designed to surface. The WOCA (Worst Outcome Contingency Awareness) test: can you save yourself with aircraft instruments and known frequencies alone?
